title: The Great Glimmerbrook Sign Mix-Up
markdown:
In Glimmerbrook the houses looked like colourful lollipops and the clouds sometimes wore silly hats. Sorrel Brightbrush painted the signs. His hair was the colour of marmalade. His hands stayed decorated with sky-blue, grass-green, and sunshine-yellow whether he liked it or not. His best friend and most opinionated assistant was Quince, a goose of discerning taste, which meant he honked approval when Sorrel got a letter straight and flapped dramatic disapproval when the paintbrush hid behind an ear, as it usually did.

One morning the village woke to a pickle. A huge, whomping wind had spent the night treating Glimmerbrook like a toy box. Trees did a wobbly dance. When villagers peeked out, every sign pointed the wrong way. Sweetie Pies Bakery, which ought to have led to Mrs. Crumble’s treats, now pointed at a grumpy badger’s burrow. Sparkle Stream Baths promised bubbly fun and indicated Farmer Giles’s mud puddle. The Giggle Garden, where flowers bloomed in funny shapes, pointed straight up, as if people might float off like balloons. Parade floats in muck, or worse, among the clouds, was not the sort of morning anyone had ordered.

The annual Grand Parade was today. Floats shaped like giant teacups, rainbow dragons, and a flying teapot were famous for arriving where they meant to. Madame Pumble, Grand Marshal, wore hats shaped like teacups that tipped when she hurried. She bustled to Sorrel’s studio, teacup hat already negotiating with gravity.

“Sorrel Brightbrush,” she boomed, surprised-owl voice in full feather. “You must fix these signs. My prize float, the Sparkling Teapot of Tidiness, will loop the post office.”

Sorrel gulped. Marmalade hair attempted a salute. Quince honked a stern note and puffed his chest until it nearly needed its own postcode.

“Right then, Quince.” Sorrel snatched the brush from behind his ear and a pot of cheerful red that smelled faintly of strawberries. “Operation Sign Salvation. First stop, Sweetie Pies.”

They zoomed off on his slightly wobbly bicycle, Quince on the handlebars offering directions that were mostly attitude. At the bakery the sign still loved the badger.

“Wrong way,” Quince honked. “Badger smells of old socks.”

The fish-market sign, which used to respect the river, swung and pointed at Quince’s nose. A surprised, slippery fish arrived on his beak. He shook. Scales sparkled like cheap jewellery.

“This wind is a prankster,” Sorrel said, wiping a scale off his cheek. He noticed a small mischievous swirl on the bakery board that he had not painted. “Like a signature,” he muttered.

They raced to Sparkle Stream Baths and found the sign now devoted to the cheese factory. The smell came out like gym socks in a sauna. Quince made a strangled sound and buried his beak in Sorrel’s smock. Then the library sign, usually quiet and sensible, spun with a wheeeek and aimed at a flock of chickens pecking a biscuit.

“We’re going to read about feathers and crumbs,” one hen announced, as if this were a reasonable timetable.

As they scurried from haywire board to haywire board, the swirls multiplied. In the wood grain, when the light hit just so, a tiny etched spiral showed, almost ethereal, as if the night itself had signed for the delivery. Sorrel stopped so suddenly Quince nearly became airborne.

“Wait. It isn’t a vandal. It’s the wind. That mighty whoosh has been nudging the signs all night, like a giant invisible puppy wagging its tail.”

Quince, having just freed a cheese crumb, looked up. “Honk?”

Sorrel’s eyes took on a new idea. Strawberry paint in the air. “If the wind likes to play, we can play back.” He did not repaint every board. Madame Pumble was a minute with a hat. For Sweetie Pies he added a jaunty extra arrow: OR the delicious pies are just past the grumpy badger’s home. (Don’t mind him. He just needs a hug.) For the baths: Or the best baths are a muddy detour away. (Embrace the squish.) For the Giggle Garden, in bouncy letters: For extra giggles, look up. You might see a cloud with a funny face. Beside his own name he painted a tiny wind-swirl, a wink to the gust, to show he understood the game.

Then the parade began. Floats followed Sorrel’s clever new directions and flowed through Glimmerbrook like a rainbow that had learned manners. People chuckled at the odd wording and still arrived where they were meant to. Not a teapot in the duck pond. Not a dragon in the turnips. Madame Pumble’s hat stopped wobbling. She laughed like tiny bells.

“You and your goose are heroes. My Sparkling Teapot of Tidiness stayed upright.”

Quince puffed and honked a triumphant trio that meant, roughly, Naturally, we are the best, and also I would like that fish back. The signs of Glimmerbrook kept their wind-approved footnotes. Sorrel wiped red from a knuckle and left the little swirls where they were, proof that a prank, answered kindly, can still get a parade home.
characters: Sorrel (sign painter), Quince (goose friend), Madame Pumble (grand marshal)
